Here, we'll introduce the last variant of ANOVA that we'll deal with: the factorial ANOVA, meaning ANOVA used with research designs that have more than one independent variable. This enables us to see not just the effect of a single variable, but how two variables interact. It's slightly more complicated, both conceptually and mathematically, but it's based on the same idea of partitioning variance that we've used in the previous two chapters.

## Social facilitation or social impairment

We've talked about the idea of social facilitation in the context of Norman Triplett's little flag racing machine. Perhaps racing head-to-head against a rival would cause the kids to race faster, amped up by the excitement and pressure of the social competition. But I mentioned something in passing which we might want to consider more carefully. In his presentation of the data, Triplett categorized some children as "stimulated positively" by the competition---those who were faster against the rival than alone. But on the other hand, some children were "stimulated adversely." Their times were worse against the rival than alone, which Triplett attributed to becoming too amped up to perform well.

So the theory has expanded to allow for both social facilitation and potential social impairment. What might account for the difference? Perhaps how easy or difficult the task is. When a task is easy, the social element could improve performance; when the task is difficult, the social pressure instead inhibits.

Consider some little kids, like Triplett's racers, but this time they're given a maze---the kind that you find in kids' activity books. Just a simple printed maze of walls, with one route to the exit that you try to trace as quickly as you can.

<!-- Each include below needs its own div: layout-ncol makes every top-level block a cell (comments too), and an unwrapped SVG gets split into pieces. -->

::: {#fig-mazes layout-ncol="2"}

:::: {}
{{< include resources/figures/maze-easy.svg >}}

:::: {}
{{< include resources/figures/maze-hard.svg >}}

Two mazes. The optimal solutions are the same length, but in the easy maze that solution is found by always choosing to go to the right. In the hard maze, that obvious choice often leads into a dead end, and you have to double back.
:::

Each maze has some branching paths---choice points---along the way. Since the exit is on the right, the obvious thing to do would be to go right every time that's an option. And the exit is right in the middle vertically, so if you're above the midpoint when you come to a choice, go down; if you're below the midpoint, go up.

What makes a maze easy or difficult? In the easy maze, those obvious choices always lead most directly to the exit. In the hard one, they don't. The hard one requires more looking ahead and overcoming that dominant, obvious response.

So say we design a study to test whether the presence of an audience affects how quickly kids can finish a maze, and whether that effect depends on the difficulty of the maze. We have two factors: maze difficulty (easy or hard) and audience (alone or watched). Each child is randomly assigned to one of the four conditions, and we measure how long it takes them to complete the maze.

Here's that kind of design with a small sample of invented data for each condition.

|  |  | **Maze** | |
|---|---|:--:|:--:|
| | | Easy | Hard |
| **Audience** | Alone | 37, 31, 42, 34 | 41, 34, 45, 40 |
| | Watched | 28, 32, 21, 31 | 53, 61, 50, 60 |

: Times (in seconds) to finish the maze for the 2×2 maze by audience design. {#tbl-factorial-data}

How does this new, more complicated design change how we analyze the data, and the conclusions we can draw? We turn once again to the logic of ANOVA, and partitioning variance. But unlike the previous chapter, where we divided the variability within groups into different components, this time we need to chop up the variability coming from the potential effects of the different treatments.

## Factorial designs

To refresh your memory of the terminology that goes with the ANOVA procedure, a factor means the variable that defines the different groups being compared, usually an independent variable that the researcher manipulates either between or within participants. The levels are the individual conditions that make up a factor.

A **factorial** design, then, is one with more than one factor, each factor with two or more levels, with every combination of those levels represented. For our purposes, we're only going to look at one kind of factorial design: the two-by-two between-participants ANOVA, which has two between-participants factors, each with two levels. But you should be aware that one or both factors can be manipulated within participants. And we can have more factors, and factors that have different numbers of levels. We could have a three-by-two within-participants design. We can even have a mix of between- and within-participants factors (called a mixed-factorial design). But again, here we'll just stick with the two-by-two between-participants version to illustrate the basic logic.

### Main effects, marginal means, and interactions

It's important to understand the basic conceptual structure. With a two-by-two design, we end up with four individual groups, one for each combination of the levels of each factor. So generically, let's say we have Factor A and Factor B. If we arrange them in a table, you can see the four conditions this creates.

|  |  | **Factor A** | | |
|---|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| | | $A_1$ | $A_2$ | *Marginal mean* |
| **Factor B** | $B_1$ | $A_1 B_1$ | $A_2 B_1$ | $M_{B_1}$ |
| | $B_2$ | $A_1 B_2$ | $A_2 B_2$ | $M_{B_2}$ |
| | *Marginal mean* | $M_{A_1}$ | $M_{A_2}$ | $M_{\text{grand}}$ |

: The four conditions of a generic 2×2 factorial design, with the marginal means for each factor in the last row and column, and the grand mean in the corner. {#tbl-factorial-generic}

If you're a participant in this study, you might be in the group of people treated with level one of Factor A and level one of Factor B. Or you might get level one of Factor A and level two of Factor B. Or you could be in level two of Factor A, level one of Factor B. Or $A_2 B_2$.[^factorial-combinations]

[^factorial-combinations]: We can find the number of individual groups by multiplying the factorial statement. So two-by-two literally means two multiplied by two, so four conditions in total. A two-by-three design would have two times three, so six groups. A three-by-five design would have three times five, so fifteen conditions. It can get pretty complicated. And you'd need a lot of participants to fill out all those subgroups. Sticking with a two-by-two design is enough for us: the logic of those more complicated designs is the same.

You'll notice that @tbl-factorial-generic also has an extra row and column labelled **marginal mean**. There's one marginal mean for each level of each factor; each is the mean of everyone at one level of a factor, ignoring the other factor. $M_{A_1}$ is the mean of all the scores in the $A_1$ column, whether they came from $B_1$ or $B_2$. Likewise, $M_{B_1}$ is the mean of all the scores in the $B_1$ row, regardless of Factor A. And in the corner is the grand mean, the mean of every score all lumped together, just as before.

When it comes to the hypothesis test for a factorial design, we'll actually run several hypothesis tests. For this two-by-two design we'll have three tests.

First, the **main effects**. The main effect of Factor A asks whether there is an overall difference between the levels of Factor A, ignoring the levels of Factor B. We just pool everyone together depending on which level of Factor A they were in, regardless of their level of Factor B. In other words, we compare the marginal means for Factor A. Then there's the main effect of Factor B. This is the same idea, applied to the other factor. We ignore the different groups on Factor A and just pool together everyone on each level of Factor B, and compare those two marginal means to see if there was an overall difference.

Third, we're interested in the **interaction** between factors A and B. This is a major reason for using a design like this, instead of just two separate studies to look at Factors A and B in isolation. We want to know if Factor A and Factor B interact---that is, if the effect of one depends on the level of the other.

Our social facilitation idea predicts just such an interaction: being watched should help on the easy maze but hinder performance on the hard maze. The effect of the audience *depends on* the difficulty of the maze.

The interaction can be the most difficult part of this analysis to really grasp. There are different patterns of results that can reflect an interaction. We'll come back to those after we run through the calculations and see the results, so we can talk it through more concretely.

### Partitioning variance in factorial designs

So for each of those three hypotheses, we calculate an $F$ ratio, and they all follow the same conceptual structure. We're comparing the variance between groups to the variance expected if there is no treatment effect. This should sound familiar. It's the same logic of the $t$ test and the other ANOVAs we've learned.

It starts out the same as every other ANOVA. We separate the total variability into variability between groups and variability within groups, each measured by its sum of squares. Here each cell of the table is a group, so our 2×2 design has four groups.

In Chapter 14, that was all the partitioning we could do. In Chapter 15, with related samples, we were able to divide up the variability within groups. Now, assuming we're just using between-participants factors, we leave the variance within groups alone and divide up the variability *between* groups instead. That's where the treatment effects are, and with two factors there's more than one of them in there. The four group means might differ because of Factor A, because of Factor B, or because of the interaction between the two. A single between-groups $F$ ratio couldn't tell those apart. It would only tell us that the four groups differ somehow. By partitioning the treatment effects, we can test each one separately.

So we want to separate between-groups variability associated with Factor A exclusively and between-groups variability associated with Factor B exclusively. And knowing both of those, anything left over---any between-groups variability not accounted for by those main effects of Factor A and Factor B---must be due to the interaction between Factors A and B.

::: {#fig-partitioning-factorial}
{{< interactive-figure factorialPartitionDiagram makeVariancePartitionDiagram options='{"preset":"factorial","formula":false,"ariaLabel":"Diagram partitioning the total sum of squares into variability between groups, which contains treatment effects and chance, and variability within groups, which contains chance. The between-groups variability is further partitioned into Factor A, Factor B, and the A-by-B interaction, each containing its own main effect or interaction plus chance."}' fallback="Diagram partitioning the total sum of squares into variability between groups, which contains treatment effects and chance, and variability within groups, which contains chance. The between-groups variability is further partitioned into Factor A, Factor B, and the A-by-B interaction, each containing its own main effect or interaction plus chance." >}}
:::

Each component gets its own $F$ ratio, always compared against the same denominator: the mean square within groups, our estimate of chance variability. As always, we get each mean square by dividing a sum of squares by its degrees of freedom.

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_A &= \frac{MS_A}{MS_{\text{within}}} \\[1.5ex]
F_B &= \frac{MS_B}{MS_{\text{within}}} \\[1.5ex]
F_{A \times B} &= \frac{MS_{A \times B}}{MS_{\text{within}}}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Sums of squares and degrees of freedom

Arriving at those $F$ ratios involves the same basic process as before. We start with between and within groups $SS$ and $df$. The equations are exactly the same as in Chapter 14. Just remember that each cell of the table is a group, so here $k = 4$.

$$
\begin{align}
SS_{\text{total}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
SS_{\text{within}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2 \\
SS_{\text{between}} &= \Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2
\end{align}
$$

$$
\begin{align}
df_{\text{total}} &= N - 1 \\
df_{\text{within}} &= N - k \\
df_{\text{between}} &= k - 1
\end{align}
$$

The new equations here are for the three pieces of the between-groups variability: the main effects and the interaction.[^factorial-equal-n] Each main effect comes from regrouping the scores by one factor, ignoring the other.

[^factorial-equal-n]: These formulas assume that every group has the same number of scores. With unequal group sizes, the pieces no longer add up so neatly, and the analysis gets more complicated. Also, as in Chapters 14 and 15, there are computational versions of these formulas. They use the total for each level of a factor in the same way that Chapter 14's used treatment totals. We'll stick with the definitional formulas.

In these equations, $M_A$ stands for each of the marginal means for Factor A in turn, one for each level: $M_{A_1}$ and $M_{A_2}$, from the bottom margin of @tbl-factorial-generic. For each one, we see how far it falls from the grand mean, square that deviation, and multiply it by $n_A$, the number of scores at that level, since each of these means represents that many scores. Then we add those up. And it's the same logic for Factor B, using the other set of marginal means, $M_{B_1}$ and $M_{B_2}$, from the right-hand margin of the table.

$$
\begin{align}
SS_A &= \Sigma n_A(M_A - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
SS_B &= \Sigma n_B(M_B - M_{\text{grand}})^2
\end{align}
$$

Notice that this is basically the same equation as for the between-groups sum of squares. The difference is that the means represent different sets of scores---all the scores at each level of one factor combined, rather than all four groups separately. We're just grouping scores one way or another to isolate different sources of variability, much like we did in Chapter 15 when we grouped the scores by person.

The degrees of freedom for each factor are its number of levels, $k_A$ or $k_B$, minus one.

$$
\begin{align}
df_A &= k_A - 1 \\
df_B &= k_B - 1
\end{align}
$$

### The interaction

And then, like I said, the $SS$ and $df$ for the interaction are simply whatever is left over: between-groups variability not already partitioned either into Factor A or Factor B. So we can find those through simple subtraction.

$$
\begin{align}
SS_{A \times B} &= SS_{\text{between}} - SS_A - SS_B \\
df_{A \times B} &= df_{\text{between}} - df_A - df_B
\end{align}
$$

For a two-by-two design, that leaves $3 - 1 - 1 = 1$ degree of freedom. More generally, it works out to $(k_A - 1)(k_B - 1)$, much like the error degrees of freedom in Chapter 15.

If you feel short-changed by the subtraction, we can also get the interaction variability directly from the data, which helps show what it represents. We give each group a prediction: the mean we'd expect for that group if the two main effects were all that was going on. To make the prediction, we start at the grand mean, then adjust for how far the mean for the group's level of Factor A is from the grand mean, and again for its level of Factor B. That simplifies to $M_A + M_B - M_{\text{grand}}$. In the table, $M_A$ and $M_B$ are the two marginal means in line with the group's cell: the one at the bottom of its column and the one at the end of its row.

The interaction is about how far each group's actual mean falls from that prediction. We square each of those differences and multiply by the number of scores in the group, just as we did for the between-groups sum of squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{A \times B} = \Sigma n_{\text{group}}(&M_{\text{group}} - M_A \\
&{}- M_B + M_{\text{grand}})^2
\end{aligned}
$$

If there were no interaction at all, every group mean would sit right on its prediction, and this would come to zero. The farther the group means are from where the main effects alone would put them, the bigger the interaction.

### One equation, different groupings

Over the last three chapters we've now used what is basically the same equation four times: group the scores, find each group's mean, and see how far those means fall from the grand mean. All that changed was the grouping. @tbl-anova-groupings lines them up, much like the table comparing the $t$ statistics in Chapter 13.

| Component | Scores grouped by | Sum of squares |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Between groups (Ch. 14--16) | Condition, or cell | $\Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ |
| Between people (Ch. 15) | Person | $\Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ |
| Factor A (Ch. 16) | Level of Factor A | $\Sigma n_A(M_A - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ |
| Factor B (Ch. 16) | Level of Factor B | $\Sigma n_B(M_B - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ |

: The same equation with the scores grouped four different ways. In each case, the squared deviation of a mean from the grand mean is multiplied by the number of scores that mean represents. {#tbl-anova-groupings}

The two new components that aren't in the table, Chapter 15's error and this chapter's interaction, came from the other move we keep making: subtracting, to see what's left of a larger component once these have been taken out.

## Factorial ANOVA in context

It's useful to lay out the process in that generic fashion, I think, but going on about "Factor A, Factor B" can feel a little abstract. Before we run through the full hypothesis test, let's just put the terms and components we just talked about into the context of our maze and audience example. Then we can see how the math works visually before actually calculating it all out.

Maze difficulty is our Factor A and audience is our Factor B. So when we come to analyze the data, we'll be grouping up the scores in different ways to analyze the different patterns of variability. For the main effect of maze difficulty, we'll be comparing everyone who did the easy maze against everyone who did the hard maze. And then for the main effect of audience, we compare everyone who worked alone with everyone who was watched. For the interaction, we're basically looking at the variability among all four cells of the table to see if anything departs from what we'd expect based on those main effects alone.

@tbl-factorial-marginal-means has the mean time for each of the four groups, with the marginal means around the edges.

|  | Easy maze | Hard maze | Audience mean |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Alone | 36 | 40 | *38* |
| Watched | 28 | 56 | *42* |
| Maze mean | *32* | *48* | *40* |

: Mean times (in seconds) for the four groups, with the marginal means for each factor in the last row and column, and the grand mean in the corner. {#tbl-factorial-marginal-means}

Kids who did the easy maze averaged 32 seconds and kids who did the hard maze averaged 48. Kids working alone averaged 38 seconds and kids being watched averaged 42. Each of those marginal means represents eight kids. And the grand mean, 40 seconds, is in the corner.

So the main effect of maze is about that 16-second difference between 32 and 48, and the main effect of audience is about the 4-second difference between 38 and 42. But look at what the audience means are hiding. Watched kids were 4 seconds slower on average, but they were 8 seconds *faster* on the easy maze and 16 seconds slower on the hard one. That's the kind of thing the interaction picks up.

<!-- Maze must remain the first factor: the explorer can label a thin second-factor layer (audience, 3% of the total), but not a thin first one. -->

::::: {#act-factorial-anova-viz .callout-tip .interactive}
## Where each effect goes

{{< interactive-figure factorialAnovaExplorer makeAnovaVariabilityExplorer options='{"stage":"populations","calculations":false,"controlsOpen":false,"factors":[{"name":"Maze","levels":["Easy","Hard"]},{"name":"Audience","levels":["Alone","Watched"]}],"groups":[{"levels":[0,0],"values":[37,31,42,34]},{"levels":[1,0],"values":[41,34,45,40]},{"levels":[0,1],"values":[28,32,21,31]},{"levels":[1,1],"values":[53,61,50,60]}],"axisLabel":"Time (seconds)","xMin":15,"xMax":65,"populationSd":4.9}' fallback="Interactive diagram of the maze-by-audience times in four groups. Total, within-groups and between-groups sums of squares are built as in Chapter 14. The scores are then regrouped by maze and by audience, and each factor's squared deviations pour into the bottom of the between-groups layer. What's left of that layer is filled by each group mean's squared distance from the mean the two factors alone predict: the interaction. Finally the maze, audience and interaction mean squares each sit over the within-groups mean square as three F ratios." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-major="scores" data-major-title="Scores" data-title="Scores" data-action='{"stage":"populations","phase":"observe","animate":false}'}
You're used to seeing data like this by now. With this 2×2 design we have four individual groups of scores, colored by the combination of maze type and audience.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="familiar" data-major-title="As before" data-title="Total" data-action='{"stage":"total","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
The first parts of the analysis are the same as the other ANOVAs we've done. We start with the total variability, which is the sum of squared deviations of every score from the grand mean.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="familiar" data-major-title="As before" data-title="Within" data-action='{"stage":"within","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
Then $SS_{\text{within}}$: the sum of squared deviations of each score from its own group mean. This is the variability that, divided by its degrees of freedom, will give us $MS_{\text{within}}$, our estimate of chance variability that provides the denominator for the three $F$ ratios we'll need.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="familiar" data-major-title="As before" data-title="Between" data-action='{"stage":"between","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
Next, $SS_{\text{between}}$: the sum of squared deviations of each group mean from the grand mean, multiplied by the number of scores in that group. Everything the maze and audience conditions did gets captured here; the new part of this factorial analysis is how we split it into the main effects and interaction.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="maze" data-major-title="Maze" data-title="Recolor" data-action='{"stage":"factor-a","phase":"recolour","animate":true}'}
First, part of the collective between-groups variability comes from any effect of maze difficulty. To quantify that separately, we group the scores by maze type, ignoring the audience factor. The scores are recolored by maze to show that new grouping.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="maze" data-major-title="Maze" data-title="Regroup" data-action='{"stage":"factor-a","phase":"rows","animate":true}'}
That gives us two groups of eight scores: everyone who did the easy maze and everyone who did the hard maze.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="maze" data-major-title="Maze" data-title="Squares" data-action='{"stage":"factor-a","phase":"squares","animate":true}'}
Those groups each have a mean (the maze factor's *marginal means*). And we can find the deviations of those means from the grand mean, just like we did for the 4 individual group means in the between-groups sum of squares.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="maze" data-major-title="Maze" data-title="Sum" data-action='{"stage":"factor-a","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
We count each square eight times, once per score in these groups. This gives the $SS_{\text{maze}}$ part of $SS_{\text{between}}$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="audience" data-major-title="Audience" data-title="Regroup" data-action='{"stage":"factor-b","phase":"rows","animate":true}'}
Now we do the same thing for the other factor, audience. We group the scores by audience, ignoring the maze, producing two new groups of 8 scores: everyone who was watched versus everyone who was unwatched.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="audience" data-major-title="Audience" data-title="Sum" data-action='{"stage":"factor-b","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
Find the deviation of each of these group means from the grand mean, square the deviations, and count each square eight times, once per score in these groups. This gives the $SS_{\text{audience}}$ part of $SS_{\text{between}}$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="interaction" data-major-title="Interaction" data-title="Left over" data-action='{"stage":"interaction","phase":"predict-start","animate":true}'}
Now we can reset back to the 4 individual groups. There is one more unclaimed part of the between-groups variability. This represents variability due to the interaction between our factors. It's whatever is left over after accounting for the main effects. We can find it through subtraction: $SS_{\text{interaction}} = SS_{\text{between}} - SS_{\text{maze}} - SS_{\text{audience}}$. Job done. But let's see what that means in a more concrete way.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="interaction" data-major-title="Interaction" data-title="Maze" data-action='{"stage":"interaction","phase":"predict-a","animate":true}'}
To quantify the interaction directly, we first predict what the individual group means would be based only on the main effects. Starting from the grand mean, the maze effect shifts the predicted means 8 seconds down for the easy maze and 8 seconds up for the hard maze, since those easy and hard marginal means were 16 seconds apart.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="interaction" data-major-title="Interaction" data-title="Audience" data-action='{"stage":"interaction","phase":"predict-b","animate":true}'}
The audience main effect shifts the predicted means 2 seconds up for the watched groups and 2 seconds down for the alone groups, since the watched and alone marginal means were 4 seconds apart. We add these adjustments to the maze prediction, so each group has a predicted mean shown as the dotted line. If there were no interaction at all, this is where the group means would be. That's not quite the case here.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="interaction" data-major-title="Interaction" data-title="Gap" data-action='{"stage":"interaction","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
Now we compare each group's actual mean with its predicted mean. Compare how? Deviations, of course! Find the deviations, square them, and add them up (counting each square $n$ times). That gives the interaction sum of squares, the part of between-groups variability that can't be explained by the main effects alone. It fills the empty portion of $SS_{\text{between}}$ exactly.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="compare" data-major-title="Compare" data-title="Partition" data-action='{"stage":"compare","phase":"partition","animate":true}'}
We started with $SS_{\text{total}}$, and split it into $SS_{\text{within}}$ and $SS_{\text{between}}$. Then we split $SS_{\text{between}}$ into the three parts: $SS_{\text{maze}}$, $SS_{\text{audience}}$, and $SS_{\text{interaction}}$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="compare" data-major-title="Compare" data-title="F" data-action='{"stage":"compare","phase":"f","animate":true}'}
The three split-up sums for the main effects and interaction get divided by their $df$ (1 in each case) to become the three separate $F$ ratio numerators. $SS_{\text{within}}$ gets divided by its $df$, and the resulting $MS_{\text{within}}$ becomes the denominator for all three.
:::
::::

:::::

## A factorial ANOVA, step by step

So now let's work through a hypothesis test for this design, using the maze and audience example in @tbl-factorial-data. Each cell had just four recorded scores.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

We need a null and alternative hypothesis for each of our three tests. For maze difficulty, the null is that the easy and hard mazes have equal population mean times, averaging across the audience conditions. For audience, the null is that the alone and watched conditions have equal population mean times, averaging across the mazes. Each alternative is that those means differ. For the interaction, the null is that the effect of being watched is the same on both mazes; the alternative is that it depends on the maze.

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

We use the same $F$ table as before, finding a critical value for each test. We'll use $\alpha = .05$ for each one. Each factor has two levels, so each main effect has $2 - 1 = 1$ degree of freedom in the numerator. The interaction also has one, which is what's left of $df_{\text{between}} = 3$ once the two main effects are taken out. And with $N = 16$ scores in $k = 4$ groups, the denominator has $df_{\text{within}} = N - k = 12$.

Here all three tests have the same numerator and denominator degrees of freedom, so they share a critical value. In @tbl-factorial-critical, the column for 1 and the row for 12 give a critical $F$ of 4.75. We'll reject the null for any of the three tests whose $F$ exceeds that value. In a more complicated between-participants design, the numerator degrees of freedom can differ, although the denominator stays the same.

::: {#tbl-factorial-critical}
{{< interactive-figure factorialCriticalTable makeFTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the maze tests","alpha":0.05,"df1":{"from":1,"to":4},"df2":{"from":10,"to":14},"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","interactive":false,"selected":{"df1":1,"df2":12,"alpha":0.05}}' fallback="F table excerpt for numerator df 1 through 4 and denominator df 10 through 14, highlighting the .05 critical value of 4.75 at F(1, 12)." >}}

An excerpt of the $F$ table, with the critical value for $df = 1$ and $12$ highlighted.
:::

Now, remember how we went out of our way to control the experiment-wise error rate in the last couple of chapters, with a single omnibus test followed by a special post-hoc test for the multiple comparisons? Well, now we're doing three $F$ tests, each at $\alpha = .05$. Are we holding the experiment-wise error rate steady at .05? Nope! The three tests' error rates pile up in exactly the way we usually try to avoid. If nothing at all were going on with our mazes and audiences, the chance of at least one of the three tests coming out significant would be about 14%, just like the three $t$ tests we worried about in Chapter 14. Why do we let that happen here? Just because! Somehow this became the accepted convention. There are statistical solutions, but a review of published research found that researchers almost never used them [@cramer2016hidden]. We'll go along with the convention for now, and come back to it when we interpret the results.

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

Again, there are a lot of values to keep track of while you calculate this, so filling in a summary table as you go is a good idea. Notice the new rows here for Factor A and Factor B and the interaction.

::: {#tbl-factorial-summary-blank .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Between groups | $\Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $k - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Factor A | $\Sigma n_A(M_A - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $k_A - 1$ | $\dfrac{SS_A}{df_A}$ | $\dfrac{MS_A}{MS_{\text{within}}}$ |
| &emsp;Factor B | $\Sigma n_B(M_B - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $k_B - 1$ | $\dfrac{SS_B}{df_B}$ | $\dfrac{MS_B}{MS_{\text{within}}}$ |
| &emsp;A × B interaction | $SS_{\text{between}} - SS_A - SS_B$ | $df_{\text{between}} - df_A - df_B$ | $\dfrac{SS_{A \times B}}{df_{A \times B}}$ | $\dfrac{MS_{A \times B}}{MS_{\text{within}}}$ |
| Within groups | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2$ | $N - k$ | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{within}}}{df_{\text{within}}}$ | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $N - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

A factorial ANOVA summary table, showing each equation.
:::

Ok, time to summit math mountain. Here's our means table again, now with each group's sum of squared deviations to save you some calculation. Below it are the sample sizes and numbers of groups and levels. From here on I'll label the components with the factor's name in place of the generic $A$ and $B$.

|  | Easy maze | Hard maze | Audience mean |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Alone | $M = 36$; $SS = 66$ | $M = 40$; $SS = 62$ | 38 |
| Watched | $M = 28$; $SS = 74$ | $M = 56$; $SS = 86$ | 42 |
| Maze mean | 32 | 48 | $M_{\text{grand}} = 40$ |

: Means and sums of squares for each cell, with the marginal means for each factor in the last row and column. {#tbl-factorial-means}

$$
\begin{gathered}
N = 16 \qquad n = 4 \qquad k = 4 \\
k_{\text{maze}} = 2 \qquad k_{\text{audience}} = 2
\end{gathered}
$$

First, the familiar components. For within groups, we can just add the four groups' sums of squares from @tbl-factorial-means:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{within}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2 \\
&= 66 + 62 + 74 + 86 \\
&= 288
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ df_{\text{within}} = N - k = 16 - 4 = 12 $$

For between groups, we find each group mean's deviation from the grand mean, square it, and multiply by the four scores it represents:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{between}} &= \Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
&= 4(-4)^2 + 4(0)^2 \\
&\quad {}+ 4(-12)^2 + 4(16)^2 \\
&= 1{,}664
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ df_{\text{between}} = k - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3 $$

Those two add up to the total: $SS_{\text{total}} = 1{,}664 + 288 = 1{,}952$, with $df_{\text{total}} = N - 1 = 15$.

Now for the new components. For the maze factor, we use the two maze means from the bottom margin of the table, 32 and 48 seconds. Each one represents eight scores:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{maze}} &= \Sigma n_{\text{maze}}(M_{\text{maze}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
&= 8(32 - 40)^2 + 8(48 - 40)^2 \\
&= 1{,}024
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ df_{\text{maze}} = k_{\text{maze}} - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1 $$

For the audience factor, we do the same with the two audience means from the right-hand margin, 38 and 42 seconds:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{audience}} &= \Sigma n_{\text{audience}}(M_{\text{audience}} \\
&\qquad {}- M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
&= 8(38 - 40)^2 + 8(42 - 40)^2 \\
&= 64
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ df_{\text{audience}} = k_{\text{audience}} - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1 $$

Then we can find the interaction by subtracting both of those from the between-groups component:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{interaction}} &= SS_{\text{between}} - SS_{\text{maze}} \\
&\quad {}- SS_{\text{audience}} \\
&= 1{,}664 - 1{,}024 - 64 \\
&= 576
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
df_{\text{interaction}} &= df_{\text{between}} - df_{\text{maze}} \\
&\quad {}- df_{\text{audience}} \\
&= 3 - 1 - 1 = 1
\end{aligned}
$$

But let's also see how the interaction builds up from the group means. Take the kids who did the easy maze alone. The mean for the easy maze is 32 and the mean for working alone is 38, so the prediction is $32 + 38 - 40 = 30$ seconds. Their actual mean was 36 seconds: 6 seconds slower than the main effects alone would suggest. @tbl-factorial-predictions does the same for all four groups.

| Group | $M_{\text{group}}$ | Prediction | Difference |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Easy, alone | 36 | $32 + 38 - 40 = 30$ | $6$ |
| Hard, alone | 40 | $48 + 38 - 40 = 46$ | $-6$ |
| Easy, watched | 28 | $32 + 42 - 40 = 34$ | $-6$ |
| Hard, watched | 56 | $48 + 42 - 40 = 50$ | $6$ |

: Each group's mean, the mean predicted from the two main effects alone, and the difference between them. {#tbl-factorial-predictions}

Every group mean is 6 seconds from its prediction, in one direction or the other. (The four differences always come out the same size with a two-by-two design with equal group sizes.) Squaring each difference and multiplying by the four scores in each group gives the same answer as before:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{interaction}} &= 4(6)^2 + 4(-6)^2 \\
&\quad {}+ 4(-6)^2 + 4(6)^2 \\
&= 576
\end{aligned}
$$

Now we have all the sums of squares and their degrees of freedom. Dividing each one by its degrees of freedom gives the mean squares:

$$
\begin{align}
MS_{\text{maze}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{maze}}}{df_{\text{maze}}} = \frac{1{,}024}{1} = 1{,}024 \\
MS_{\text{audience}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{audience}}}{df_{\text{audience}}} = \frac{64}{1} = 64 \\
MS_{\text{interaction}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{interaction}}}{df_{\text{interaction}}} = \frac{576}{1} = 576 \\
MS_{\text{within}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{within}}}{df_{\text{within}}} = \frac{288}{12} = 24
\end{align}
$$

Finally, we divide each of the three new mean squares by the within-groups mean square:

$$
\begin{align}
F_{\text{maze}} &= \frac{MS_{\text{maze}}}{MS_{\text{within}}} = \frac{1{,}024}{24} \approx 42.67 \\
F_{\text{audience}} &= \frac{MS_{\text{audience}}}{MS_{\text{within}}} = \frac{64}{24} \approx 2.67 \\
F_{\text{interaction}} &= \frac{MS_{\text{interaction}}}{MS_{\text{within}}} = \frac{576}{24} = 24.00
\end{align}
$$

Here's the completed summary table:

::: {#tbl-factorial-summary .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Between groups | 1,664 | 3 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Maze (A) | 1,024 | 1 | 1,024 | 42.67 |
| &emsp;Audience (B) | 64 | 1 | 64 | 2.67 |
| &emsp;Interaction (A × B) | 576 | 1 | 576 | 24.00 |
| Within groups | 288 | 12 | 24 | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | 1,952 | 15 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

Completed factorial ANOVA summary table for the maze × audience example.
:::

That wasn't so bad, right? Hopefully you're seeing how ANOVA supplies a consistent set of principles by which we can chop up and analyze data. It's a bit of a pain to do by hand, and researchers these days use software to do the calculations for them. But it's worth working through the math at least once to reinforce how this kind of ANOVA works behind the scenes.

{{< include quizzes/16-factorial-anova-calculate-2x2.qmd >}}

### Step 4: Make a decision

The maze and interaction $F$ ratios both exceed the critical value of 4.75, so we reject those two null hypotheses. The audience $F$ does not, so we fail to reject its null.

<!-- FIGURE (2026-11-09): new, modeled on Chapter 14's fig-anova-decision, with all three Fs on one curve. Fine on desktop; on a phone the Audience and 4.75 labels sit close together at the left edge. Shorter labels or a narrower x-axis would help if it stays. -->

::: {#fig-factorial-decision}
{{< interactive-figure factorialTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"f","df1":1,"df2":12,"title":"Null distribution: F(1, 12)","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[0,45],"yDomain":[0,1],"clipPlot":true,"xTicks":6,"labels":{"x":"F ratio"},"shade":{"tail":"right","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":4.747225,"label":"4.75","height":0.45,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":2.666667,"label":"Audience","height":0.75,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"},{"at":24,"label":"Interaction","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"},{"at":42.666667,"label":"Maze","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null F distribution with 1 and 12 degrees of freedom. The rejection region lies above 4.75. The observed F for audience, 2.67, falls short of it; the observed Fs for the interaction, 24.00, and for maze, 42.67, are far into the rejection region." >}}

The three observed $F$ ratios against the null $F$ distribution with $df = 1$ and $12$. Audience ($F = 2.67$) falls short of the critical value; the interaction ($F = 24.00$) and maze ($F = 42.67$) are well beyond it.
:::

Kids took significantly longer on the hard maze overall. The average difference between being watched and working alone wasn't significant. But the significant interaction tells us that this average doesn't tell the whole story: the effect of being watched depends on which maze the kids did.

### Step 5: Estimate the effect and follow up

#### Effect size: partial $\eta^2$

We also estimate an effect size for each test, whether or not it was significant. As in Chapter 15, we'll use partial eta squared: one for maze, one for audience, and one for the interaction.

In each case, the numerator is the $SS$ for that component of the variability and the denominator is the partial variability, excluding the other sources that we quantify separately. So for the main effect of maze, we set aside the $SS$ for audience and for the interaction, just as we dumped $SS_{\text{people}}$ out of the bucket in Chapter 15. What's left is $SS_{\text{maze}}$ plus $SS_{\text{within}}$, and we ask what proportion of that is $SS_{\text{maze}}$. The same rule applies to audience and the interaction: each denominator contains just that effect's $SS$ plus $SS_{\text{within}}$.

$$
\begin{align}
&\text{Maze:} \\[0.5ex]
&\quad \eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{\text{maze}}}{SS_{\text{maze}} + SS_{\text{within}}} \\[0.5ex]
&\quad \phantom{\eta^2_p} = \frac{1{,}024}{1{,}024 + 288} = .78 \\[2ex]
&\text{Audience:} \\[0.5ex]
&\quad \eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{\text{audience}}}{SS_{\text{audience}} + SS_{\text{within}}} \\[0.5ex]
&\quad \phantom{\eta^2_p} = \frac{64}{64 + 288} = .18 \\[2ex]
&\text{Interaction:} \\[0.5ex]
&\quad \eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{\text{interaction}}}{SS_{\text{interaction}} + SS_{\text{within}}} \\[0.5ex]
&\quad \phantom{\eta^2_p} = \frac{576}{576 + 288} = .67
\end{align}
$$

These three proportions have different denominators, so they aren't shares of one total and don't need to add up to 1.

#### Simple effects

In the last two chapters, this is where we followed a significant $F$ with post-hoc tests. We don't need them for our main effects: each factor only has two levels, so if there's a difference, there's only one place it can be.^[With three or more levels of a factor, a significant main effect would leave the same question open as in Chapter 14, and we could follow it up the same way, with a test like Tukey's HSD.] The interaction does need some additional probing, though. It tells us that the effect of being watched isn't the same on both mazes, but not what the effect *is* on either one. Watched kids were 8 seconds faster than kids working alone on the easy maze, and 16 seconds slower on the hard maze. Is each of those a reliable difference in its own right?

To find out, we test **simple effects**: the effect of one factor at a single level of the other. Here that means comparing the alone and watched means twice, once for the easy maze and once for the hard maze. Mathematically, there's nothing new. Each simple effect is just a between-groups sum of squares for two of our four groups: the means of 36 and 28 seconds around the easy-maze mean of 32, and the means of 40 and 56 around the hard-maze mean of 48. Two means give $df = 1$, so each mean square is the same as its sum of squares. And we divide by the same $MS_{\text{within}}$ as before, since it's still our best estimate of chance variability, based on all sixteen kids.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Easy maze:} \\
&\quad SS = 4(36 - 32)^2 + 4(28 - 32)^2 = 128 \\
&\quad F = \frac{128}{24} \approx 5.33 \\[1.5ex]
&\text{Hard maze:} \\
&\quad SS = 4(40 - 48)^2 + 4(56 - 48)^2 = 512 \\
&\quad F = \frac{512}{24} \approx 21.33
\end{aligned}
$$

With $df = 1$ and $12$, the critical value is the same 4.75 as before, and both $F$ ratios are beyond it.^[The two sums of squares add up to 640, which is exactly $SS_{\text{audience}}$ plus $SS_{\text{interaction}}$, $64 + 576$. The simple effects haven't found any new variability. They've taken everything the audience did, the main effect and the interaction together, and split it up by maze instead.] So being watched made kids significantly faster on the easy maze, and significantly slower on the hard maze. Both halves of the pattern are significant at the unadjusted .05 threshold.

We could have sliced the interaction the other way, testing the effect of the maze for kids working alone and for kids being watched. That would tell us that the hard maze took 4 seconds longer than the easy one for kids working alone, which isn't a significant difference ($F = 1.33$), and 28 seconds longer for kids being watched, which is ($F = 65.33$). It's the same interaction seen from the other side, and it's an accurate description of the data. But it only tells us that an audience widens the gap between the mazes. It can't tell us whether that's because watched kids sped up on the easy maze, slowed down on the hard one, or both. And that's exactly what our theory makes predictions about: facilitation on the easy task and impairment on the hard one. So we let the research question choose which simple effects to test.

One caution. Testing every simple effect we can think of would bring back the experiment-wise error rate problem from Chapter 14, and even our two follow-up tests add to it. There are corrections we could apply if we were being fastidious. Our easy-maze result, with $p = .040$, is close enough to the threshold that it might not survive one. The hard-maze result would.

#### Statistical power

The logic of power is the same as in @act-anova-power, but here we need to plan for the effect we're interested in detecting. A study can have enough power to detect a main effect and still miss an interaction. For our question, we'd plan the sample size around how much the audience effect might differ between the two mazes, along with the variability within groups and our chosen alpha. Four kids per cell make a manageable teaching example; real studies generally need more.

## Reporting and interpreting results

### Reporting results

As always, we report the design and what we measured, followed by the $F$ ratios, degrees of freedom, $p$ values, and effect sizes for all three tests. The four group means are usually easier to follow in a table or graph than crammed into a sentence. Here they're in @tbl-factorial-means and @fig-maze-results. We also report the simple effects used to follow up the interaction.

> To examine the influence of maze difficulty and an audience on performance, a 2-factor ANOVA was conducted with completion times as the dependent variable and Maze Difficulty and Audience as between-participants independent variables. There was no significant main effect of Audience ($F(1, 12) = 2.67$, $p = .128$, $\eta^2_p = .18$). There was, however, a significant main effect of Maze Difficulty ($F(1, 12) = 42.67$, $p < .001$, $\eta^2_p = .78$); overall, times were longer on the hard maze. Moreover, there was a significant interaction between Maze Difficulty and Audience ($F(1, 12) = 24.00$, $p < .001$, $\eta^2_p = .67$); the effect of being watched depended on maze difficulty. Unadjusted simple-effects tests showed faster times when watched on the easy maze ($F(1, 12) = 5.33$, $p = .040$) and slower times when watched on the hard maze ($F(1, 12) = 21.33$, $p < .001$).

@fig-maze-results shows the four means with either factor on the x-axis. Remember that lower times mean faster performance.

:::: {#fig-maze-results}
::: {.sfs-figure-row .sfs-figure-row-wide .sfs-maze-results-row}

{{< interactive-figure mazeResultsByAudience makeInteractionPlot options='{"means":{"a1b1":36,"a2b1":40,"a1b2":28,"a2b2":56},"factorA":"Maze","factorB":"Audience","yLabel":"Mean time (seconds)","xTickLabels":["Easy","Hard"],"seriesLabels":["Alone","Watched"],"yDomain":[0,60],"yTicks":"numeric","valueLabels":true,"controls":false,"swapAxes":true,"width":440}' fallback="The same four means with audience on the x-axis and one line per maze. Easy maze: 36 seconds alone, 28 watched. Hard maze: 40 seconds alone, 56 watched. The lines do not cross, but they are not parallel." >}}
:::
The four mean times, graphed two ways: with maze on the x-axis and a line for each audience condition, and with audience on the x-axis and a line for each maze.
::::

Each dot is a group mean, and each line joins the means for one level of the other factor. In the left graph, the solid line for kids working alone rises only a little from easy to hard; the dashed line for watched kids rises steeply. In the right graph, the easy-maze line falls from alone to watched, while the hard-maze line rises. The lines cross in the first graph and don't in the second, but they're non-parallel in both. The interaction is the same whichever way we graph it.

### Interpreting the results

Our results show one possible pattern. What else might we have found, and how would we recognize it? The next figure shows how to read the main effects and interaction from the graph, then tries some other patterns. These are patterns in the means; the $F$ tests tell us whether they're statistically significant.

::::: {#act-maze-interaction .callout-tip .interactive}

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="key" data-major-title="Our result" data-title="Our result" data-action='{"means":{"a1b1":36,"a2b1":40,"a1b2":28,"a2b2":56},"show-lines":true,"highlight":"none","marginals":"none","prediction":false,"animate":false}'}
Start with our four group means, with maze on the x-axis and one line for each audience condition. Let's find the two main effects and the interaction on this graph.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="key" data-major-title="Our result" data-title="Maze" data-action='{"means":{"a1b1":36,"a2b1":40,"a1b2":28,"a2b2":56},"show-lines":true,"highlight":"none","marginals":"a","prediction":false,"animate":true}'}
The hollow diamonds sit midway between the two means for each maze. They're the marginal means: 32 seconds for easy and 48 for hard. The dotted line joining them slopes up, showing the overall difference associated with maze difficulty.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="key" data-major-title="Our result" data-title="Audience" data-action='{"means":{"a1b1":36,"a2b1":40,"a1b2":28,"a2b2":56},"show-lines":true,"highlight":"none","marginals":"b","prediction":false,"animate":true}'}
Now the hollow markers sit at the middle of each audience line: 38 seconds alone and 42 watched. That 4-second gap is the overall audience difference. It is small compared with the differences within each maze, because those go in opposite directions and partly cancel out.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="key" data-major-title="Our result" data-title="Prediction" data-action='{"means":{"a1b1":36,"a2b1":40,"a1b2":28,"a2b2":56},"show-lines":true,"highlight":"none","marginals":"none","prediction":true,"animate":true}'}
The faint parallel lines show what the two main effects alone predict, using the same means we calculated in @tbl-factorial-predictions. Each observed mean is 6 seconds from its prediction. Those departures are the interaction: the audience difference changes between mazes instead of staying the same.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="whatif" data-major-title="What if?" data-title="Nothing" data-action='{"means":{"a1b1":40,"a2b1":40,"a1b2":40,"a2b2":40},"show-lines":true,"highlight":"none","marginals":"both","prediction":false,"animate":true}'}
From here on, we'll replace our results with other possible patterns. First, all four means are equal. The lines lie flat on top of each other: no maze difference, no audience difference, and no interaction.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="whatif" data-major-title="What if?" data-title="Maze only" data-action='{"means":{"a1b1":32,"a2b1":48,"a1b2":32,"a2b2":48},"show-lines":true,"highlight":"none","marginals":"both","prediction":false,"animate":true}'}
Here there's a main effect of maze only. Both audience lines climb together, one on top of the other. The maze marginal means differ, but the audience marginal means are equal, and the lines are parallel.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="whatif" data-major-title="What if?" data-title="Audience only" data-action='{"means":{"a1b1":34,"a2b1":34,"a1b2":46,"a2b2":46},"show-lines":true,"highlight":"none","marginals":"both","prediction":false,"animate":true}'}
Here there's a main effect of audience only. Both lines are flat, so the maze marginal means are equal. Being watched adds the same amount of time on either maze: an audience difference, but no interaction.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="whatif" data-major-title="What if?" data-title="Both" data-action='{"means":{"a1b1":26,"a2b1":42,"a1b2":38,"a2b2":54},"show-lines":true,"highlight":"none","marginals":"both","prediction":false,"animate":true}'}
Now both main effects are present. The lines slope up from easy to hard and are separated vertically. They're still parallel: being watched adds the same 12 seconds on either maze, so there's no interaction.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="whatif" data-major-title="What if?" data-title="Fanning out" data-action='{"means":{"a1b1":30,"a2b1":34,"a1b2":30,"a2b2":54},"show-lines":true,"highlight":"none","marginals":"both","prediction":false,"animate":true}'}
Here the audience makes no difference on the easy maze but adds 20 seconds on the hard one. That's an interaction, even though the lines don't cross. Both main effects are present too: the hard maze takes longer overall, and so does being watched.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="whatif" data-major-title="What if?" data-title="Crossover" data-action='{"means":{"a1b1":30,"a2b1":50,"a1b2":50,"a2b2":30},"show-lines":true,"highlight":"none","marginals":"both","prediction":false,"animate":true}'}
Here there's an interaction without either main effect. The audience effect reverses between mazes, but the opposite differences cancel out when we calculate the marginal means. The diamonds' line is flat, and the two audience midpoints coincide. Neither main effect captures how much the conditions matter in combination.
:::
::::

:::::

{{< include quizzes/16-factorial-anova-interpreting-results-1.qmd >}}

Our made-up kids showed the predicted pattern: facilitation on the easy task and impairment on the hard one. Because we randomly assigned kids to the four conditions, the design lets us investigate whether being watched causes those changes.

The idea that task difficulty changes the effect of an audience is associated with Robert Zajonc. A review of 241 studies found that real people broadly showed the predicted pattern, though the effects were much smaller than ours [@bond1983social]. Zajonc and his colleagues also ran a famous study with cockroaches doing a straight runway or a more complicated maze [@zajonc1969social]. But their analysis never separately tested the audience-by-task interaction. A preregistered replication with three times as many roaches in that comparison found that an audience slowed them down on both tasks: two significant main effects, but no significant interaction [@halfmann2020replicating].

The replication's preregistration identified the interaction as the critical test. Which brings us back to our three tests at .05 each. Our central question was about the interaction too. If we'd committed to that one test up front and used it alone to judge that prediction, its Type I error rate would be .05. The ANOVA still hands us the two main effects, but those aren't extra chances to declare our prediction supported. Preregistration doesn't remove the multiple-testing problem if we still treat any significant result as a success [@cramer2016hidden].

### Assumptions

The assumptions are the same as in Chapter 14, applied to all four cells: independent observations, approximately normal population distributions within each cell, and equal population variances across cells. The equal-variance assumption is also what lets us use the pooled $MS_{\text{within}}$ for the simple-effects tests.

## Practice: Design your own example

Now come up with an example of your own, or describe a study you've learned about that fits this two-by-two between-participants design. Name two independent variables, each with two levels, and one dependent variable. Then sketch the pattern you'd predict: four dots for the group means, joined into two lines. You don't need exact numbers; relatively high or low is enough. Finally, explain what your predicted main effects and interaction would mean in terms of your study.
